synopsis: Open-source simulators are viable low-license-cost cores for heavy off-road automatic-braking validation, but not the lowest-total-cost option: coupling, assets, scenarios and validation evidence still require specialist labor, potentially producing a seven-figure annual program [f196, f8303, f8318]. Expert judgment supports a narrow first-release toolchain if work starts in October 2026 and existing simulators are reused; precedents include MineSim, published in April 2025 for autonomous mining trucks, and AutoDRIVE-based vision-guided AEB testing across 128 simulated off-road cases [f1591, f464, f467]. Capabilities differ materially: Chrono offers deformable-soil models, MAVS has validated tire-soil and lidar-vegetation models, while CARLA has a mining earth-mover asset but no soil physics [f3739, f3740, f15901, f15902]. These capabilities do not establish safety-case credibility: CARLA, Gazebo and Isaac Sim were not verified in this research, none was found validated for off-road collision warning, and open-source availability alone does not establish verification, validation or applicability [f5850, f5851, f7758]. Planning should account for separate asset-license terms, freeze a qualified build as projects change, and investigate maintenance and security-patch arrangements, which the research did not examine [f8908, f15936, f15938, f9392, f9393].
